opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core intuition is pretty simple: a lot of the risk from very capable AI systems doesn't start when the model is released to the public. It starts the moment it's being used inside the lab. And right now, most frontier safety policies are framed around external deployment. The trigger is roughly "before we put this in the API or ship it in a product, we run our dangerous capability evals and check our mitigations." That made a lot of sense a couple of years ago, but I think it's increasingly the wrong mental model.

If you look at how labs actually operate, the most capable models are typically used internally first, sometimes for months, and often with fewer restrictions than the public version. Employees get access to helpful-only variants, models get hooked up to internal codebases, given access to compute, used as coding agents on the lab's own infrastructure. And the explicit goal of a lot of these labs is to use AI to accelerate AI research itself. So the place where you'd expect the most capable, most autonomous, least constrained use of a model is precisely inside the company.

And that's where a few of the threat models I care most about live. One is scheming or deceptive alignment: if a model has misaligned goals and is reasonably situationally aware, the most leveraged place for it to act is inside the lab, where it might be writing code for the next training run, touching monitoring systems, or interacting with its own weights. Sabotaging safety research, inserting subtle backdoors, trying to exfiltrate itself: those are all internal deployment risks. You don't need a public release for any of that to go wrong.

The second is the runaway dynamic around automated AI R&D. If internal models are substantially speeding up research, you can get pretty rapid capability jumps that the outside world, and even parts of the company, don't really see. If your evaluation trigger is "external release," you might go through several generations of increasingly capable systems without ever hitting a formal checkpoint.

Then there's a more boring but important set of issues: security and misuse by insiders, model weights being stolen, and so on. An internally deployed model with strong cyber capabilities is a security concern regardless of whether customers ever see it.

So concretely, what I'd want is for frontier safety policies to say: the evaluation and mitigation requirements apply at the point of significant internal use, not just at external release. That means running dangerous capability evals, and importantly also evals for things like scheming propensity and situational awareness, before a model is widely used internally, especially in agentic settings with access to sensitive systems. It means having control measures in place, like monitoring of what internal agents are doing, access restrictions, logging, and the ability to audit after the fact. And ideally there's some transparency about this to external parties, like governments or third-party evaluators, because otherwise there's this growing gap between what the public thinks frontier AI looks like and what actually exists inside the labs.

I don't think this is a particularly radical ask. It's mostly just closing a gap that already exists in how these policies are written. But I think it's one of the more important gaps, because as AI systems get more capable and more autonomous, the inside of the lab is increasingly where the action is.

r001.rationale: The response says policies are framed around external deployment and calls internal evaluation a gap to close; it does not say internal-model evaluation was already implicit.

r002.rationale: It calls for evaluating scheming propensity and situational awareness before widespread internal use, so companies understand relevant behavioral propensities.

r003.rationale: It recommends transparency to external parties, including governments, about the growing gap between public understanding and what exists inside labs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic argument is pretty simple. Most of the frontier safety policies that labs have published are framed around external deployment. The trigger for an evaluation is "we're about to release this model to the public," or "we're about to give API access to customers." And that made sense when the main worry was misuse by outsiders. But I think the threat model has shifted, or at least it has broadened, and the policies haven't fully caught up.

The thing that worries me most is that the most capable model at any given lab, for most of its lifetime, is not externally deployed. It's used internally. It's being used to write code, to run experiments, increasingly to help with the next round of AI research itself. And that internal usage is exactly the setting where some of the scariest failure modes live. If a model is going to try to sabotage safety research, or insert a backdoor into the training code, or exfiltrate its own weights, or just subtly steer the research agenda in a direction that's good for it and bad for us, that's not going to happen through the public API. It's going to happen inside the lab, with a model that has a lot of permissions and is talking to a lot of internal infrastructure.

So if your safety policy says "we evaluate before external deployment," you've built a system where the highest-stakes deployment doesn't get the evaluation. That seems backwards to me.

And there's a second thing, which is that internal deployment is where the capability is actually being used to do the thing we're most worried about, which is accelerating AI development. If you believe in any version of the "AI automates AI research" story, then the moment that starts happening in earnest is a moment of really high consequence. You'd want to know what the model's propensities are before you give it broad access to your codebase and your compute, not after. The standard "we'll check at release" framing just doesn't engage with that.

I also think there's an incentive problem that makes this worse. Internal deployment is quiet. There's no press release, there's no customer-facing launch, there's often no clean line where someone says "okay, this model is now deployed." It's a gradual ramp. Researchers start using the new checkpoint, it works better, more people use it, it gets wired into more tools. And nobody ever made a deployment decision, so nobody ever triggered the evaluation. That's not malice on anyone's part, it's just how organizations work. Which is exactly why you want the policy to be explicit about it. If you leave it implicit, the default outcome is that it doesn't happen.

Now, I want to be fair about the counterargument, because I think there's a real one. Labs will say internal deployment is lower risk because it's a small number of people, they're monitored, they're trusted, and the model is sandboxed. And some of that is true. But I'd push back on a couple of those. "Trusted users" doesn't help you if the concern is the model, not the user. And "sandboxed" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. In practice, internally deployed models often have more access than externally deployed ones, not less. They can see the training code, they can see the eval code, sometimes they're literally helping write the next evals. That's about the worst place to have a model with bad intentions and no checks.

So what I'd want to see concretely is fairly modest. Define internal deployment in the policy. Say what counts as a model being used internally at scale, and have that be a trigger for the same kind of capability and propensity evaluations you'd run before a release. Scale the scrutiny with the affordances: a model that's helping with autonomous research should get more scrutiny than one that's answering questions in a chat window. And have some monitoring in place so that if you're wrong about the model, you have a chance to notice.

The honest version of this is that none of the current evals are good enough that passing them means you're safe. But that's true of external deployment too, and we still think it's worth doing. The point of putting it in the policy is less about the specific tests and more about making the lab actually look. Right now, for internal models, a lot of labs just aren't looking. And I think that's a gap that's going to matter more every year.

r001.rationale: The response says policies focus on external deployment and that internal evaluations are often not triggered; it does not say internal evaluation was already implicit.

r002.rationale: It calls for policy-triggered capability and propensity evaluations before broad internal access, so labs understand models’ behavioral propensities.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest informing governments about internally deployed models’ capabilities or propensities.

astra-6.text:
Because a model can pose serious risks before it’s ever released to the public. If you deploy it internally to do AI research, write code, or operate tools, it may have access to sensitive information and opportunities to take consequential actions. So public release is not the only point at which you need to ask whether a model is safe.

Imagine using a new model to substantially accelerate the development of the next generation. You’d want to understand both whether it could undermine your oversight and whether that acceleration could take you beyond what your existing safety measures can handle. Keeping the model inside the company doesn’t, by itself, resolve either concern.

That’s why the policies should explicitly cover internal deployment. They should specify what evaluations are required, what findings would trigger additional safeguards, and when a particular use should be paused. Otherwise, you can have a policy that looks strong on public releases but misses consequential uses that happen earlier.

r001.rationale: The response argues that policies should explicitly cover internal deployment, but does not say evaluating these models was already implicit in existing policies.

r002.rationale: It calls for evaluations of internal deployments and discusses oversight and acceleration risks, but does not clearly require companies to understand models’ behavioral propensities.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest informing governments about internally deployed models’ capabilities or behavioral propensities.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a model can have a huge impact even if it’s never released to the public. If you deploy it internally to do AI research, write code, or help train the next generation of models, you’re already exposing yourself to some of the risks that a frontier safety policy is supposed to address.

For example, you might have a model that’s capable of undermining your security or interfering with the research you’re relying on to assess whether the next model is safe. And if it substantially accelerates AI development, you could move into a much more dangerous capability regime before your safeguards are ready.

So I think the relevant question is: what can the model do, what access does it have, and how are you using it? Whether it’s available through a public API is only one part of that. If your policy only requires evaluations before external deployment, you leave a potentially very consequential gap. You want evaluations before significant internal use, and safeguards that reflect the risks of that use.

r001.rationale: The response argues that policies should require evaluations before significant internal use, but does not say that evaluating internal models was already implicit in existing policies.

r002.rationale: It discusses models’ capabilities, access, and risks, but does not clearly state that companies should understand their behavioral propensities.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest informing governments about internal models’ capabilities or behavioral propensities.
